name: Online Shopping and Banking Safely
objectives: Given an online store or deal, check the store with three checks before buying: a real web address, reviews and complaints, and the return policy, with all three checks done and a clear buy or do-not-buy decision
At a store's payment page, choose a payment method that protects you and explain why, never choosing gift cards, wire transfers, payment apps or crypto for an online seller
After placing an order, keep the order records, track the package from the store's own site or app and start a return, with the confirmation kept and no tracking done from links in surprise texts
Using your bank's official app or website, sign in safely and check your balance and recent transactions, reaching the bank without a link from an email or text, and signing out at the end
Given your list of recent transactions, identify a charge you did not make and describe the steps to report it and lock the card, calling the number on the card or official app and acting quickly
Given a call, text or email about your money, identify the signs of a money scam and stop it, never giving a password or code and always calling back on the number on your card

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Checking that a store is real
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check a website before you buy from it.
This lesson builds toward: Given an online store or deal, you will check the store with three checks before buying: a real web address, reviews and complaints, and the return policy, with all three checks done and a clear buy or do-not-buy decision.
Fake stores copy the look of real ones and advertise prices that are too good to be true. Before you buy, take a minute to check.
Type the store's address yourself, or use its official app, instead of clicking an ad or a link in a text. Look at the address bar: is the name spelled right? Look for https and a lock, but know that the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) warns scammers can use these too.
The FTC suggests searching the store or product name with the word "complaint" or "scam" to see what other buyers say, reading reviews with care since some are fake, and checking the return policy before you buy: how many days you have, and who pays to send it back.
Step by step:
- Type the store's address yourself or use its official app.
- Check the spelling of the web address.
- Search the store name plus "complaint" or "scam".
- Read several reviews, not just the stars.
- Read the return policy: how many days, and who pays return shipping.
Words to know:
- Web address: the name of a website, shown in the bar at the top of the browser, like target.com.
- https: a sign that the connection to a site is protected; scammers can use it too.
- Return policy: the store's rules for sending things back.
Official sources:
- FTC: Online shopping
Try it now: Pick a store you might buy from. Do the three checks: search its name with "complaint", read three reviews, and find how many days you have to return an item.
You can now check a store's address, reputation and return policy before you buy.

check.q: What should you check in the address bar before you buy?
options: The color of the page
How many items are in the cart
The time of day
That the store's name is spelled right
check.why: Fake stores often use look-alike names, so check the spelling.

check.q: You see an ad on social media for shoes at a very low price. What would you do?
options: Type the store's address yourself and search its name with "complaint" or "scam"
Click the ad and pay right away
Send the seller a gift card
Share your card number in a message
check.why: Going to the store yourself and searching for complaints helps you spot fake stores.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Paying the safer way
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose a payment method that protects you if something goes wrong.
This lesson builds toward: At a store's payment page, you will choose a payment method that protects you and explain why, never choosing gift cards, wire transfers, payment apps or crypto for an online seller.
How you pay matters. The FTC says paying by credit card gives you strong protection: you can dispute a charge that is wrong, for something that never arrived or was not as described. Act fast and tell your card company as soon as you see a problem.
The FTC warns never to pay an online seller with gift cards, wire transfers, payment apps or cryptocurrency. These are hard to get back, which is why scammers ask for them.
Type your card details only on the payment page of a store you have checked, never in an email, text or chat. On a shared or library computer, do not let the browser save your card.
Step by step:
- Use a credit card when you can, or a trusted checkout from the store you checked.
- Never pay a seller by gift card, wire transfer, payment app or cryptocurrency.
- Type card details only on the checked store's payment page.
- Do not save your card on a shared computer.
- Watch your statement and report problems quickly.
Words to know:
- Credit card: a card that borrows money you pay back later; it has strong protections for disputes.
- Dispute: telling your card company a charge is wrong so it can look into it.
- Wire transfer: sending money directly from one account to another; very hard to get back.
Official sources:
- FTC: Online shopping
Try it now: Look at the cards and payment methods you have. Write which one you would use to buy online and why, and which methods you would refuse if a seller asked.
You can now choose the payment method that protects you and refuse the ones scammers ask for.

check.q: What does it mean to dispute a charge?
options: To pay it twice
To ask your card company to fix a wrong charge
To send the seller a gift card
To delete your account
check.why: With a credit card you can dispute a charge for something wrong or that never arrived.

check.q: An online seller says they only accept a wire transfer. What would you do?
options: Send the wire transfer
Pay half by wire and half by gift card
Do not buy; the FTC warns never to pay online sellers this way
Pay with cryptocurrency instead
check.why: Wire transfers are hard to get back, which is why scammers ask for them.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Tracking, receiving and returning an order
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Keep your order records, track a package and start a return.
This lesson builds toward: After placing an order, you will keep the order records, track the package from the store's own site or app and start a return, with the confirmation kept and no tracking done from links in surprise texts.
After you buy, the store sends an order confirmation by email. Keep it. The FTC suggests keeping your order details, the return policy, the seller's shipping promise, your messages with the seller and your payment statement.
Track the package from your account on the store's website or app, not from a link in a surprise text. Fake "delivery problem" texts are a common scam.
To return something, sign in to your account, find the order, and choose return. Follow the steps, keep the receipt from the drop-off, and watch for the refund on your statement. If the seller will not fix a problem, you can report it to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov.
Step by step:
- Save the order confirmation email.
- Track the package from your account on the store's site or app.
- Ignore surprise delivery texts with links.
- To return: sign in, find the order, choose return, follow the steps.
- Keep the drop-off receipt and check for the refund.
Words to know:
- Order confirmation: the email that proves what you bought and what you paid.
- Tracking: following where your package is on its way to you.
- Refund: money given back to you.
Official sources:
- FTC: Online shopping
- FTC: Report fraud
Try it now: Find an order confirmation email in your inbox (or one from a past purchase) and make an email folder or label called "Orders" to keep it in. If you have an open order, track it from the store's own app or site.
You can now keep order records, track a package safely and start a return.

options: A text asking you to pay a fee
An ad for a new product
The email the store sends after you buy
A bank statement
check.why: The store emails an order confirmation; keep it with your records.

check.q: You dropped off a return at the post office. What would you do next?
options: Throw away the receipt
Buy the item again
Delete the store's app
Keep the drop-off receipt and watch for the refund on your statement
check.why: The receipt proves you sent it back, and the statement shows the refund.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Using your bank's app or website safely
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Sign in to your bank's official app or website and check your balance and transactions.
This lesson builds toward: Using your bank's official app or website, you will sign in safely and check your balance and recent transactions, reaching the bank without a link from an email or text, and signing out at the end.
Online banking lets you see your balance, check what has been paid in and out, pay bills and move money between your own accounts, from your phone or computer.
Get the bank's app only from the official app store, and check the developer is your real bank. Or type the bank's web address yourself; find it on your card, statement or by asking at the branch. Never sign in from a link in an email or text.
Use a strong password used nowhere else and turn on two-step verification. Do not bank on public Wi-Fi without your phone's own data, and always sign out when you finish, especially on a shared computer.
Step by step:
- Install the official bank app or type the bank's address yourself.
- Sign in with a strong, unique password.
- Turn on two-step verification in security settings.
- Look at your balance and recent transactions.
- Sign out when you finish.
Words to know:
- Balance: how much money is in your account now.
- Transaction: one payment in or out of your account.
- Two-step verification: a second check, usually a code sent to your phone, when you sign in.
Try it now: Open your bank's official app or website (type the address yourself). Sign in, look at your balance and your last five transactions, then sign out.
You can now sign in to your bank safely and check your balance and transactions.

check.q: Where can you find your bank's real web address?
options: On your card, your statement or by asking at the branch
In a text that says your account is locked
In an ad on social media
In an email from someone you do not know
check.why: Your card, statement and branch give the bank's real address.

check.q: You checked your balance on a library computer. What would you do before you leave?
options: Leave the page open
Sign out
Save your password in the browser
Write your password on a note
check.why: Always sign out when you finish banking, especially on a shared computer.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Spotting a wrong charge and knowing your money is protected
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Review your transactions and know what to do about a charge you did not make.
This lesson builds toward: Given your list of recent transactions, you will identify a charge you did not make and describe the steps to report it and lock the card, calling the number on the card or official app and acting quickly.
Check your transactions at least once a week. Look for charges you do not recognize, even small ones; thieves sometimes test a card with a tiny charge first. Many banks let you turn on alerts that text or email you when money leaves your account.
If you see a charge you did not make, call the number on the back of your card or in the official app, and act quickly. Many cards and apps let you lock or freeze the card right away.
Money in a bank insured by the FDIC is protected up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, for each account ownership category. Credit unions insured by the NCUA have the same $250,000 standard limit. The FDIC says crypto assets, stocks, bonds and mutual funds are not insured, even when sold by a bank.
Step by step:
- Review transactions every week.
- Turn on account alerts in the app.
- If a charge is not yours: lock the card in the app if you can.
- Call the number on the back of your card.
- Watch for the bank's follow-up and check your next statement.
Words to know:
- Alert: a text or email your bank sends when something happens on your account.
- FDIC: the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, which insures money in US banks.
- NCUA: the National Credit Union Administration, which insures money in US credit unions.
Official sources:
- FDIC: Understanding deposit insurance
- NCUA: Share insurance coverage
Try it now: In your bank app, find where alerts are set up and turn on an alert for payments. Then find the button that locks or freezes your card (do not press it unless you need to).
You can now check your transactions, set alerts, and act quickly on a charge you did not make.

check.q: Why should you look at small charges you do not recognize?
options: Small charges are always fine
Banks never make mistakes
Small charges are free
Thieves sometimes test a card with a tiny charge first
check.why: A tiny unknown charge can be a test before bigger ones.

check.q: You want to know right away when money leaves your account. What would you do?
options: Check once a year
Ask a stranger to watch it
Turn on alerts in your bank's app so it texts or emails you
Close your account
check.why: Many banks offer alerts when money leaves your account.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Money scams: fake bank calls and payment app tricks
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Recognize a money scam and stop it.
This lesson builds toward: Given a call, text or email about your money, you will identify the signs of a money scam and stop it, never giving a password or code and always calling back on the number on your card.
A common scam: someone calls, texts or emails pretending to be your bank's fraud team. They say your account is in danger and ask for your password, a code sent to your phone, or for you to move money to a "safe account". A real bank will never ask for these.
The FTC lists four signs of a scam: they pretend to be someone you trust, there is a problem or a prize, they pressure you to act now, and they want payment in an unusual way, like gift cards, wire transfers, payment apps or cryptocurrency.
If in doubt, hang up. Call the number on the back of your card. Treat money sent through payment apps like cash: send it only to people you know. In the United States, report scams at reportfraud.ftc.gov.
Step by step:
- Never share your password or a code sent to your phone.
- Never move money to a "safe account" because a caller says so.
- Hang up and call the number on the back of your card.
- Send payment app money only to people you know.
- Report scams at reportfraud.ftc.gov.
Words to know:
- Impersonation: pretending to be someone else, like your bank or a government office.
- Payment app: an app that sends money from person to person, like Venmo, Cash App or Zelle.
Official sources:
- FTC: How to avoid a scam
- FTC: Report fraud
Try it now: Final task practice: write the phone number from the back of your bank card in a safe place at home. Then do the final task: check a store, choose your payment method, and review your bank transactions.
You can now spot a fake bank call or payment app trick, stop it, and report it.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Checking the store Fewer than three checks were done, or the store was reached from an ad or text link. All three checks done: real web address, reviews and complaints, and the return policy. Also notes how many days you have to return the item and who pays to send it back. Payment choice No payment method chosen, or gift card, wire, payment app or crypto chosen. Chooses a protective method such as a credit card and says why. Also says not to save the card on a shared computer. Checking the bank account Signed in from a link, or could not find the balance or transactions. Signs in through the official app or a typed address and finds the balance and recent transactions. Also turns on two-step verification or alerts, and signs out. Wrong charge plan No plan, or the plan uses a number from a text or email. Says they would lock the card and call the number on the card or official app quickly. Also says they would check transactions every week and keep records for a dispute. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What will a real bank never ask you for?
options: To visit a branch
Your password or the code sent to your phone
To check your statement
To turn on two-step verification
check.why: A real bank will never ask for your password, a code, or to move money to a "safe account".

check.q: A text from "your bank" says your account is in danger and to call a number in the text. What would you do?
options: Ignore the number in the text and call the number on the back of your card
Call the number in the text
Reply with your password
Move your money to the account they give you
check.why: Calling the number on your card reaches your real bank.
